summary: Updates RFC 3261 to fix a SIP vulnerability where a few legitimate requests can cause huge amounts of traffic between forking proxies. It strengthens loop-detection requirements for proxies that fork requests and corrects the description of the loop-detection algorithm. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Imagine a message that, whenever it is copied and passed around, makes more copies that go in circles. This fixes the rules so helpers notice loops and stop the flood.

subtitle: A few SIP requests could set off exponential proxy traffic. This update requires loop detection when forking and adds Max-Breadth.

tldr.problem: A SIP proxy that forks a request to several destinations can be tricked into passing it round a loop, so fewer than ten messages could stimulate potentially 2^71 messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5393 requires a forking proxy to make sure a request is not looping, and corrects RFC 3261's loop-detection algorithm using a two-part Via branch value. It also adds a Max-Breadth header field that caps concurrent forked branches.
tldr.outcome: Loop detection and Max-Breadth blunt the attack, but a determined attacker with enough distinct resources can still cause a lot of traffic, spread over a longer time. The RFC says further protocol work is needed.

today: RFC 5393 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states that further protocol work is needed against attackers with many distinct resources.

sections.title: The Forking Amplification Attack
sections.content:
Interoperability testing found that forking SIP proxies, as defined in RFC 3261, can turn a small number of valid requests into an enormous number of proxy-to-proxy messages. Consider two proxy/registrar services P1 and P2 with four Addresses of Record (AORs). Each AOR registers both AORs of the other service as contacts. An INVITE to a@P1 then forks to two requests at P2, which fork to four at P1, then eight, and so on.

The requests keep spreading until Max-Forwards reaches zero. With RFC 3261's recommended settings the tree is 70 rows deep, representing 2^71-1 requests, and each proxy would hold state for at least 2^70 simultaneously active transactions near the end. The attack can even be set up with one REGISTER request to one account, by registering contacts that differ only in URI parameters such as unknown-param=whack and unknown-param=thud.

The scenario was realized at a SIP Interoperability Test (SIPit) session, where proxies capped Max-Forwards at 20 and bombarded each other. A fork branch could also point at a victim that is not even SIP-aware.
sections.eli5: Two post offices each forward every letter to two other addresses, which send it back doubled. Soon there are more letters than anyone can count.

sections.title: Required Loop Detection
sections.content:
When a proxy forks a request to more than one location, it MUST ensure that the request is not looping through it. Using the loop-detection steps in this document is RECOMMENDED, which leaves room for future mechanisms. For example, a proxy forking to destinations set up with the sip-outbound mechanism would know those branches cannot loop.

A proxy forwarding to just one location MAY perform loop detection but is not required to, because the amplification risk is absent and Max-Forwards still protects the network.
sections.eli5: Any helper who makes copies must check that a copy has not already been through its hands.

sections.title: The Corrected Loop-Detection Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC replaces item 8 of Section 16.6 and item 4 of Section 16.3 of RFC 3261. A proxy required to detect loops SHOULD build the branch value of its Via header field in two parts. The first part satisfies RFC 3261 Section 8.1.1.7. The second part MUST vary with every field the location service uses to decide where to forward, so it MUST depend at least on the received Request-URI and any Route header field values used. It MUST NOT vary with the request method.

Before forwarding, the proxy inspects each Via value whose sent-by matches one it placed earlier. If the second part is present, the proxy recomputes it for the current request. Equal values mean the request has looped and the proxy MUST reject it with a 482 (Loop Detected) response. Different values mean the request is spiraling, and processing continues.

The cost is order n^2 as a message crosses n proxies, in place of exponential growth. For the second part, the RFC suggests hashing the Request-URI, Route values and other location-service inputs, for example CRC-32c or MD5, plus a field like Call-ID or CSeq. It warns that removing or changing another node's branch values prevents that node from detecting loops.
sections.eli5: Each helper stamps a code on the letter based on where it is sending it. If the same code comes back, it is going in circles and gets stopped.

sections.title: Max-Breadth
sections.content:
Loop detection alone is not enough when many AORs fork to each other, because paths take a long time to loop. With N such AORs the traffic exceeds N! even if every proxy detects loops. So the RFC defines the Max-Breadth header field, a single positive integer that limits how many concurrent branches a forked request may spawn.

A proxy that receives no Max-Breadth MUST add one, RECOMMENDED to be 60. Each proxy has a maximum allowed incoming value, also RECOMMENDED to be 60, and overwrites larger values. When forwarding, the proxy divides its value among outgoing requests and MUST NOT let the Outgoing Max-Breadth (the sum over forwarded requests without a final response) exceed the Incoming value. When a branch gets a final response its share is freed for reuse. A proxy that cannot do a needed parallel fork, and cannot fork serially or redirect, MUST return 440 (Max-Breadth Exceeded).

Max-Breadth is independent of Max-Forwards: it never counts down per hop and does not limit depth. A value of 1 means forking must be serial, not that it is forbidden. A user agent server ignores the field, and a user agent client MAY set it, RECOMMENDED to be 60.
sections.eli5: Each helper is told how many copies can be out at once. When a copy comes back finished, they may send another.

sections.title: Limits and Rejected Alternatives
sections.content:
Max-Breadth does not reduce the total traffic of the attack. It only spreads it out by capping concurrency, so operators should watch for gradual growth in outstanding transactions and be able to disable resources used in an attack. Gateways, including SIP-to-SIP back-to-back user agents, that strip history information can create loops that neither Max-Forwards, loop detection nor Max-Breadth can stop.

Alternatives considered and rejected were relying on legal action, a smaller Max-Forwards cap, disallowing registration bindings to arbitrary contacts, deprecating forking, and not reclaiming breadth from completed branches.
sections.eli5: The new rules slow the flood and make it easier to spot, but a clever and determined cheater with lots of addresses could still cause trouble.

sections.title: New Header Field and Response Code
sections.content: The RFC registers the Max-Breadth header field, with no compact form, in the Header Fields sub-registry of the SIP Parameters registry. It also registers response code 440 with the default reason phrase "Max-Breadth Exceeded" in the Response Codes sub-registry. The header's syntax is Max-Breadth = "Max-Breadth" HCOLON 1*DIGIT.
sections.eli5: The new rule and the new "too many at once" message are added to the official lists of SIP words.
